subject: fennec
pitch: A fennec fox kit standing alert on a little sand dune at dusk. Enormous satin ears lined in pale peach, cream fur warming to sandy gold along its back, a fluffy tail with a smudge of black at the tip, and big dark eyes with a tiny white sparkle. Its paws are a touch oversized, like it hasn't grown into them yet, and it wears a woven leather collar with a small brass bell.
reasoning:
I need to write a correct TypeScript module using the SDK, keeping it concise but functional. For the subject, I'm thinking of a fennec fox kit scaled realistically—body around 0.2m, ears 10-15cm, so an overall stylized model size of roughly 0.3m.

Now I'm defining the color palette (cream, gold, peach, black, brass, sand tones) and sketching the skeleton: hips, spine chain, neck, and head joints positioned to give the fox a short-legged stance atop a sand dune base resting at y=0.

Still structuring the spine chain and joint hierarchy...

Actually simpler is better: I'll sweep the body along the spine chain itself, using a radius function that tapers from rear to front, and apply a countershaded paint going from gold on the back to cream on the belly.

For the head, I'm shaping it as a scaled sphere plus a tapered snout swept along a small curve with a dark nose tip at the end. I'm working out how to orient the head joint so it tilts forward without getting tangled in local coordinate confusion, deciding to keep the aim target simple rather than overthink the bone direction math.

Now I'm placing big dark eyes symmetrically on the face using mirrored x offsets, with small white sparkle spheres for highlights, and planning out the enormous fennec-style ears as extruded leaf-shaped outlines anchored near the top of the head, sized appropriately large for the character.

I'm working out the ear's orientation and thickness so it tilts outward and back rather than sitting flat, then coloring it with a cream-gold outer surface and softer peach inner lining to give it a satiny look.

I'll simplify: faces get a cream-gold tone and the thin edges get painted peach, using the thickness direction vector (cross product of the x and y axes) to distinguish face from rim.

Now I'm positioning the ears at the top-back of the head, tilted outward, with a leaf-shaped outline that tapers to a rounded tip and thickness tapering from base to tip with a slight bevel. Then I'm moving on to the tail, planning a fluffy chain swept along a catmull-rom curve running back from the hips.

I'm shaping the tail radius to bulge fatter in the middle using a sine function and taper at the tip, then setting up a black-to-gold gradient near the tip using sampled points along the tail path.

Now I'm turning to the legs: oversized paws, four limbs attached at shoulder/hip sockets on the sides of the body, with feet resting on a sand dune. I'm modeling the dune as a flattened sphere and checking whether its lowest point sinks too far below the floor, since scenery pieces may need to respect the same floor-contact constraint as the main model.

Working out foot placement on the dune surface, estimating the sphere-profile height at each paw position so the legs land naturally sinking slightly into the sand rather than floating above it.

For the limbs themselves, I'm sizing hip-to-foot distances and choosing segment lengths so each leg comfortably reaches its target with a bend: front legs get a simple two-segment knee bend forward, while hind legs need three segments (hip-knee-hock-foot) with the hock bending backward for a proper digitigrade stance.

Figuring out the leg chain structure now — using three-named chains to create shoulder/elbow/wrist joints with hips as parent, then sweeping tubes along each chain with tapering radius and adding paw spheres at the tip joint positions.

Working out the paw placement: sizing them with a squashed sphere scale, offsetting forward and setting the y-position so they sink slightly into the dune surface rather than floating above it, aiming for bottoms around 0.046 against dune heights near 0.05-0.06.

Now I'm computing the leg geometry — shoulder and foot points for front and hind limbs, checking distances against chosen segment lengths so the limb reaches without overextending, and setting bend directions for natural knee/elbow flexion. I'm also defining the leg radius as a sweep function for tapering thickness along each limb.

For coloring, I'm assigning a darker gold to the legs with cream paws, and using a countershade function on the body to blend gold on the back with cream on the belly. For the spine, I'm laying out a chain of points from hips through mid-spine to chest, with a radius function that varies sinusoidally to give the torso a rounded, slightly tapered silhouette before connecting into the chest and head joint.

I'm continuing the skeleton with a neck segment leading into a head sphere that's scaled to be slightly flattened and elongated, placing cream cheek fluff spheres on either side, then sweeping a tapered muzzle shape forward from the head bone and capping it with a small dark nose sphere.

Now I'm positioning the eyes on the sides of the head so they protrude slightly past the head sphere's surface for visibility, adding small white sparkle highlights offset forward on each eye, and starting to work out the base position for the ears near the top of the head.

I'm figuring out the orientation vectors for the ears, debating between making them face forward (thin from the side) versus facing outward sideways (wide silhouette from the side, thin from front) to best match a fennec fox's large side-visible ears, and considering a tilted compromise between the two.

Working out the diagonal thickness vector for the ear plane, I'm using it to determine how to paint the ear faces — distinguishing outer (gold/cream), inner (pale peach), and rim colors based on the dot product between the face normal and this tilted axis.

I work out that multiplying the dot product by the side sign gives a consistent outer/inner test, so outer faces get the gold-cream color and inner faces get peach. Now I'm moving to the collar: I need to figure out the neck ring placement by sampling the spine chain near t≈0.8 to locate the neck center point, then building a ring of points around it for the woven leather collar geometry.

Writing collar sweep points...

Now adding the bell: a small brass sphere hanging at the collar's front with a tiny torus loop to attach it, assigned to the neck bone so it moves with the spine joint. I'll keep fur accents minimal, maybe skipping extra tufts to keep things modest.

For the tail, I'm setting up a chain of joints running from the hips backward and curving upward at the tip, with a radius function that tapers from thick at the hips to fluffy mid-tail and narrows again near the end. I'm shading it with a soft gradient darkening toward a black smudge at the very tip for a natural countershaded look.

For the body, I'm applying a countershade effect with gold along the back fading to cream on the belly and sides, and keeping the paws and legs cream-toned. I'm also noting what imports I actually need—builder, curve functions, paint, countershade, gradient, mottle—and planning the final export block with a name and description for the creature.

Now I'm setting up the color palette and starting the main build function, defining joints and a catmull-spline spine chain from hips upward.

Next I'm sweeping the body along the spine with a countershaded gold-to-cream gradient, then placing the head joint at the top of the spine and working out how to orient it using an aim direction toward the forward position.

For the head itself, I'm skipping the aim parameter so it inherits the parent spine joint's orientation, then adding a flattened sphere for the skull with a scale that stretches it slightly, painted with the same countershaded coat as the body. I'm adding cream cheek spheres on either side, sweeping a tapering muzzle shape forward from the face using a curved path, and starting on a small nose sphere at the tip.

Now I'm placing the eyes as scaled spheres on both sides with tiny white highlight dots, then working out the ear geometry by computing a tangent direction to determine which side of each ear should be colored as the outer ear versus the inner peach color, using a dot product test against a normal vector.

I'm sketching the ear outline as a curved, symmetrical shape with sharp corners at the base and rounded smoothing toward the tip, then extruding it with a slight thickness and bevel so it reads as large, floppy fox ears.

I'm defining the leg geometry using a limb helper that takes root, foot, and segment lengths plus bend directions to create jointed chains for front and hind legs, naming each joint so I can attach paw spheres and tiny toe bumps at the tips, sized to feel oversized and chunky.

I'm building the tail as a curved chain through four control points, then sweeping a tube along it with a radius that bulges in the middle and tapers with a sine function, applying a gradient color that fades from gold to black near the tip for a fluffy, smudged look.

I'm constructing a collar as a closed ring of points around the neck, sized to sit just outside the neck's spine radius, then sweeping a tube along it with a woven stripe pattern and attaching a small brass bell sphere at the front where the collar dips lowest.

Finally I'm shaping a sandy dune base using two overlapping flattened hemisphere lobes with a mottled sand texture, checking that the height under each paw roughly matches where the feet would sink in, and considering (then skipping) extra fur tufts or texture details to keep things simple.
